lessonTitle: Condensation: Film Correlations, Condensate Rate and Dropwise Comparison

blocks.text: The condenser of a 600 MW steam turbine rejects roughly 400 MW of heat while holding steam at about 5 kPa, and every extra kelvin of condenser temperature costs measurable output. Because steam on cold tubes forms a liquid film whose thickness controls the whole heat transfer rate, the condensation coefficient decides how big and how expensive that condenser must be.

blocks.markdown: **Condensation** occurs when vapour contacts a surface below its saturation temperature $T_{sat}$. Latent heat is released at the vapour-liquid interface and must conduct through the condensate to the wall at $T_s$. The driving temperature difference is $\Delta T = T_{sat}-T_s$ (K). In **film condensation** the liquid wets the surface and forms a continuous film; in **dropwise condensation** the liquid does not wet the surface and forms discrete droplets that grow, coalesce and roll off, leaving bare surface between them.

blocks.title: Condensate film and the Nusselt model
blocks.text: Nusselt (1916) analysed a laminar condensate film on a vertical plate. He assumed a thin film, gravity-driven flow balanced by viscous shear, conduction-only heat transfer across the film, negligible vapour shear and constant properties. The film thickens with distance $x$ down the plate, so the local coefficient $h_x\propto x^{-1/4}$ decreases down the plate.

blocks.markdown: Heat flux through the film is $q''=k_l\Delta T/\delta$, where $\delta(x)$ is the local film thickness (m) and $k_l$ is the liquid conductivity (W/m K). The film grows because condensate accumulates, so $\delta$ increases with $x$ and $h_x=k_l/\delta$ falls. Averaging over a plate of height $L$ gives the standard laminar-film result below, in which $h'_{fg}=h_{fg}+0.68\,c_{p,l}\Delta T$ (J/kg) corrects the latent heat for sub-cooling of the condensate. Liquid properties are evaluated at the film temperature $(T_{sat}+T_s)/2$, and $h_{fg}$ and $\rho_v$ at $T_{sat}$.

blocks.caption: Average coefficient (W/m$^2$ K) for laminar film condensation on a vertical plate of height $L$

blocks.title: Direction of the effects
blocks.text: $\bar h_L$ increases with $k_l$, with $\rho_l$ and with $h'_{fg}$, and decreases with viscosity $\mu_l$. It decreases as the plate height $L$ or the temperature difference $\Delta T$ increases, both as a power of $-1/4$, because a taller plate or a larger flux produces a thicker film. It never depends on the wall material, only on the film.

blocks.title: Film coefficient and condensate rate on a vertical plate
blocks.prompt: Saturated steam at 1 atm condenses on a vertical plate 0.050 m tall and 0.300 m wide held at 96 $^\circ$C ($\Delta T=4$ K). Typical properties: $h_{fg}=2257$ kJ/kg, $\rho_v=0.596$ kg/m$^3$; liquid at film temperature 98 $^\circ$C: $\rho_l=960$ kg/m$^3$, $k_l=0.679$ W/m K, $\mu_l=2.9\times10^{-4}$ Pa s, $c_{p,l}=4215$ J/kg K. Find $\bar h$, the heat rate and the condensate flow.

steps.text: Correct the latent heat for sub-cooling.
Evaluate the bracket in Nusselt's formula.
Heat rate and condensate rate, with area $A=0.050\times0.300=0.0150$ m$^2$.
Check the film Reynolds number, $Re_\delta=4\dot m/(w\mu_l)$ with width $w=0.300$ m, to confirm the laminar assumption.

blocks.answer: $\bar h\approx17.2$ kW/m$^2$K, $Q\approx1032$ W and $\dot m\approx0.45$ g/s, with $Re_\delta\approx21<30$ so the film is laminar and wave-free.

rows: Continuous liquid film in series with wall
Droplets on bare surface, very thin average resistance
Often 5 to 10 times higher, up to 100 000 W/m$^2$K or more
Promoters wear off, coverage fades, so films are assumed for design
blocks.caption: Typical comparison for steam; values are representative, not guaranteed.

blocks.markdown: The condensate **rate** follows from an energy balance. All the latent heat released must be removed by the coolant, so the heat duty $Q$ (W) equals the condensate mass flow $\dot m$ (kg/s) times the latent heat. In design the duty is usually known first, and the rate of condensate to be drained and returned follows directly.

blocks.latex: \dot m_c=\frac{Q}{h_{fg}}\quad\text{(or } Q/h'_{fg}\text{ if sub-cooling is included)}

blocks.title: Condensate rate from a heat duty
blocks.prompt: A process condenser must remove 1.50 MW from saturated steam at 1 atm (latent heat 2257 kJ/kg). How much condensate is produced per hour, assuming the condensate leaves at saturation?

steps.text: Convert duty to watts and divide by latent heat.

blocks.answer: About 0.665 kg/s, or roughly 2393 kg/h (2.4 t/h) of condensate to be drained.

items: Non-condensable gases such as air accumulate at the interface and can cut condensation coefficients severely, so condensers are vented.
On horizontal tubes the film is thinner and the Nusselt tube result uses a diameter in place of height with a different constant (about 0.729).
Vapour shear and film waves (above $Re_\delta\approx30$) raise the coefficient above the Nusselt value, so Nusselt is a conservative estimate.
Turbulent film flow occurs at $Re_\delta$ above roughly 1800 and requires different correlations.

blocks.title: Do not size for dropwise
blocks.text: Dropwise condensation is rarely sustained in industry. Size equipment on film condensation and treat any dropwise benefit as unreliable extra margin.

points: Nusselt's laminar film model gives $\bar h_L=0.943[\rho_l(\rho_l-\rho_v)g h'_{fg}k_l^3/(\mu_l\Delta T L)]^{1/4}$, decreasing with $L$ and $\Delta T$.
Condensate rate follows from the energy balance $\dot m=Q/h_{fg}$ (or with $h'_{fg}$).
Dropwise condensation gives coefficients several times larger than film condensation because there is no continuous liquid resistance, but it is unreliable in practice.
Check the film Reynolds number to confirm the laminar, wave-free assumption.

questions.stem: For laminar film condensation on a vertical plate, how does the average heat transfer coefficient change if the plate is made four times taller, at the same $\Delta T$ and fluid?

options.text: It increases by a factor of 4, because more surface condenses more vapour
It decreases by a factor of 4, because it varies as $L^{-1}$
It decreases by a factor of about 1.41, because it varies as $L^{-1/4}$
It is unchanged, because the film properties do not depend on the plate height

questions.correctOptionText: It decreases by a factor of about 1.41, because it varies as $L^{-1/4}$

distractorRationale.a: Total heat rate rises with area, but the average coefficient falls because the film thickens.
distractorRationale.d: Film thickness accumulates down the plate, so height matters.

questions.explanation: The Nusselt result contains $L^{-1/4}$, so quadrupling $L$ divides $\bar h$ by $4^{0.25}=1.414$. The film is thicker on average over a taller plate, and thicker film means more conduction resistance.

questions.stem: Why does dropwise condensation usually give a much higher heat transfer coefficient than film condensation on the same cooled surface?

options.text: The vapour is hotter in dropwise condensation, so the driving temperature difference is larger
Droplets have much higher thermal conductivity than a liquid film
Dropwise condensation releases more latent heat per kilogram of vapour
There is no continuous liquid layer in series with the wall, because droplets grow, coalesce and roll off leaving bare metal exposed to vapour

questions.correctOptionText: There is no continuous liquid layer in series with the wall, because droplets grow, coalesce and roll off leaving bare metal exposed to vapour

distractorRationale.a: The vapour is at saturation in both cases; the difference is the surface liquid arrangement.
distractorRationale.b: Conductivity is the same liquid property; the benefit comes from removing the film thickness.
distractorRationale.c: Latent heat is a fluid property at saturation and does not depend on the condensation mode.

questions.explanation: The film in film condensation acts as a conduction resistance in series between vapour and wall. In dropwise condensation most of the wall is bare and drops are small, so the average resistance is much lower and coefficients are often 5 to 10 times larger.

questions.stem: For a vertical plate with laminar film condensation, the local heat transfer coefficient is largest at the top of the plate where the condensate film is thinnest.
questions.explanation: At the top the film thickness starts from zero, so $h_x=k_l/\delta$ is very large and then falls as $\delta$ grows down the plate as $x^{1/4}$. The average coefficient over height $L$ is therefore $4/3$ times the local value at the bottom of the plate.

questions.stem: A condenser removes 340 kW from saturated steam at 2 bar, for which the latent heat is 2202 kJ/kg. Calculate the condensate mass flow rate in kg/s, assuming condensate leaves at saturation.
questions.explanation: The duty is released entirely as latent heat, so the mass flow is Q/h_fg = 340 000/2 202 000 = 0.1544 kg/s, about 556 kg/h. Using the sub-cooling correction would change this by well under one percent here.

questions.stem: Steam at 0.2 bar condenses on a vertical plate 0.30 m tall held 8 K below saturation. Use the Nusselt expression with typical properties: h_fg = 2358 kJ/kg, vapour density 0.13 kg/m^3, liquid density 985 kg/m^3, conductivity 0.651 W/m K, viscosity 4.9e-4 Pa s, specific heat 4183 J/kg K. Find the average heat transfer coefficient in W/m^2 K.
questions.explanation: First h'fg = 2 358 000 + 0.68 x 4183 x 8 = 2380756 J/kg. The group rho_l(rho_l-rho_v) g h'fg k^3/(mu dT L) is 5.315e+15, whose fourth root is 8538.5, so h = 0.943 x 8538.5 = 8052 W/m^2 K. This is a laminar-film value; the film is thin because the temperature difference is small.

questions.stem: A vertical plate 0.5 m tall gives an average condensing coefficient of 5200 W/m^2 K at a temperature difference of 10 K. Assuming the Nusselt laminar-film scaling holds and all property variations are negligible, what is the coefficient for a plate 1.0 m tall at a temperature difference of 20 K? Give the answer in W/m^2 K.
questions.explanation: The coefficient scales as (L dT)^(-1/4), and L dT changes by a factor of 2 x 2 = 4. The new value is 5200 x 4^(-1/4) = 3677 W/m^2 K, a reduction of about 29 percent because both a taller plate and a larger flux thicken the film.

questions.stem: A designer must remove 2.4 MW with a surface held 12 K below saturation. Film condensation would give about 6 kW/m^2K and dropwise about 30 kW/m^2K. What are the required areas, film then dropwise?

options.text: About 6.7 m$^2$ for film and 33 m$^2$ for dropwise
About 33 m$^2$ for film and 6.7 m$^2$ for dropwise
About 3 m$^2$ for film and 0.6 m$^2$ for dropwise
About 33 m$^2$ for both, because the duty fixes the area

questions.correctOptionText: About 33 m$^2$ for film and 6.7 m$^2$ for dropwise

distractorRationale.a: The larger coefficient needs the smaller area; the two have been swapped.
distractorRationale.c: The temperature difference has been used twice or ignored; area equals $Q/(h\Delta T)$.
distractorRationale.d: The area depends on the coefficient through $Q=hA\Delta T$.

questions.explanation: The area is $A=Q/(h\Delta T)$. For film this is 2.4e6/(6000 x 12) = 33.3 m$^2$ and for dropwise 2.4e6/(30000 x 12) = 6.7 m$^2$. A five-fold larger coefficient shrinks the required area five-fold at the same temperature difference.

questions.stem: In the Nusselt vertical-plate result, the effective latent heat $h'_{fg}=h_{fg}+0.68c_{p,l}\Delta T$ is used instead of $h_{fg}$ alone. What does the extra term account for?

options.text: Sub-heating of the vapour above saturation before it condenses
Radiation from the wall to the vapour
The kinetic energy of falling condensate
Sub-cooling of the condensate below saturation, which also has to be removed from the film

questions.correctOptionText: Sub-cooling of the condensate below saturation, which also has to be removed from the film

distractorRationale.a: The model assumes saturated vapour; superheat is not the subject of this correction.
distractorRationale.b: Radiation is neglected in the Nusselt model.
distractorRationale.c: Kinetic energy is neglected; the term is a sensible-heat correction.

questions.explanation: As condensate flows down the cold wall it is cooled below saturation, so more energy than the latent heat leaves per kilogram. The factor 0.68 reflects the temperature profile in the film and the correction is usually a few percent of $h_{fg}$.

questions.stem: Explain why, for laminar film condensation on a vertical plate, the local coefficient decreases down the plate, and state how the average coefficient responds to increases in wall subcooling $\Delta T$ and in liquid viscosity.
markingGuide: Condensate accumulates so film thickness $\delta$ increases with distance down the plate
Heat is transferred by conduction across the film, so $h_x=k_l/\delta$ falls as $\delta$ grows
Larger $\Delta T$ drives more condensation and a thicker film, so $\bar h$ decreases as $\Delta T^{-1/4}$
Higher viscosity slows the draining film, making it thicker so $\bar h$ decreases as $\mu_l^{-1/4}$
States that heat rate still rises with $\Delta T$ because $Q=\bar hA\Delta T$ increases as $\Delta T^{3/4}$
questions.explanation: The film thickens because more condensate must be carried by the film further down, and conduction resistance rises with thickness. Larger subcooling and larger viscosity both slow drainage relative to production, so the film is thicker and the coefficient lower.

questions.stem: A steam condenser is being designed on film condensation. A colleague suggests applying a dropwise promoter and reducing the planned surface area by a factor of ten. Discuss the benefit and the risk, and say what basis you would use for the design.
markingGuide: States that dropwise condensation can give coefficients several times higher (5 to 10 times typical) because there is no continuous liquid film resistance
Explains droplets nucleate, grow, coalesce and roll off, exposing bare surface
Notes the need for a non-wetting surface, the loss of promoter or coating with time, and fouling or oxidation returning the surface to film mode
Notes that the overall resistance also includes the coolant side and wall, so a tenfold area cut is not justified by the condensing coefficient alone
Concludes to design on film condensation with dropwise as an unquantified margin
questions.explanation: The condensing-side coefficient is only one resistance in the overall coefficient, and dropwise operation cannot be guaranteed for the life of the plant. A prudent design therefore uses film condensation values and treats any dropwise improvement as bonus margin.
